meeting_transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Rina Patel (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (Verdant SRE), Tomás Alvarez (Verdant Head of ML), Priya Kapoor (Verdant Platform Eng)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive; focused on designing a surge-absorber tier to protect reserved GPU pools during large bursts. Discussed queueing model (M/M/c vs G/G/c approximations), admission control, prewarmed pools, KV cache warmup, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem network egress considerations.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: ok everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro? we've got about an hour, aiming to walk through a proposed surge-absorber design and then go into the queueing sims.
[00:08] Anika Rao: yep hi, Anika here, i'll be the SRE touchpoint, we manage the kubernetes clusters in our private datacenter and the load patterns are... uh, spiky.
[00:13] Tomás Alvarez: Tomas, head of ML, hi. our production flows have periodic daytime spikes and occasional bulk re-score jobs. main ask: keep user-facing latency below 250 ms p95 while not overcommitting GPUs.
[00:23] Luis Ortega: ok, cool. quick note: from Redwood side Rina and I will walk through runtime behavior (kv cache, batching) then get into admission and queueing.
[00:30] Rina Patel: yep. quick question before we dive — are you planning private deployment (on-prem) for all traffic or a hybrid (some hosted)?
[00:36] Priya Kapoor: Primarily on-prem in our VPC for compliance reasons. we might route non-sensitive bulk jobs to hosted later.
[00:42] Maya Chen: makes sense. so the design we're proposing is a two-tier model: an edge surge-absorber made of prewarmed, low-capacity pods that handle immediate short bursts and a reserved GPU pool behind it for sustained load.
[00:55] Anika Rao: by prewarmed pods you mean smaller instances with, like, a warm kv cache? how do we warm the cache without spending insane GPU minutes?
[01:02] Rina Patel: good question — we differentiate between prefix warm and KV warm. prefix warm is basically keeping model weights in memory (preloaded) whereas KV warm is populating the attention KV caches for common conversation prefixes. we recommend caching top N prefixes from your trace and keeping a tiny LRU for others.
[01:22] Tomás Alvarez: right, but our long-tail prompts cause a lot of kv cold starts — that’s where p95 spikes. how much does prewarming reduce latency in practice, for like a 4k context?
[01:30] Luis Ortega: from our internal sims, warm KV on a compatible quantized 4-bit path reduces generation latency by ~20-30% on p95; on 16k it’s more pronounced. but two caveats: (1) warm KV memory overhead grows with active sessions, (2) quantization can increase token throughput but sometimes slightly shifts sampling behavior.
[01:50] Priya Kapoor: about quantization — are you recommending 4-bit quant for our reserved pools? we care about reproducibility for reranking.
[01:56] Rina Patel: we usually recommend mixed strategy: 8-bit for critical rerank paths where deterministic behavior matters, 4-bit for bulk inference when throughput is king. also you can keep a small set of model variants pinned for specific endpoints.
[02:10] Anika Rao: ok. walk us through the admission control / queueing model. we've been using a naive FIFO queue and it fails under burst.
[02:16] Luis Ortega: we propose a prioritized admission controller: immediate short-burst service from the surge-absorber up to X concurrent requests, then probabilistic admission for the reserved pool based on queue depth and estimated latency tail. modeled as an M/G/c with state-dependent arrival — not perfect but workable.
[02:32] Tomás Alvarez: M/G/c — did you compare with Erlang-C or G/G/c approximations? Erlang-C seems to overestimate waits for highly bursty arrival streams.
[02:39] Luis Ortega: yes, Erlang-C is optimistic for memoryless assumptions. we ran trace-based discrete-event sims using your exported traffic and compared: Erlang-C underpredicted p95 in 3 of 4 heavy-burst windows. trace-driven sim was the gold standard.
[02:52] Maya Chen: one pattern we like: use a ticketing system — tokens represent capacity in reserved pools. surge-absorber returns a probability-weighted admission token. if no token, requests are short-circuited to a degraded response or queued with exponential backoff.
[03:05] Priya Kapoor: degraded response — do you mean shorter completions, fewer tokens generated, or a cached answer?
[03:10] Rina Patel: could be any of those. typical approach: for chat, fall back to a condensed response template; for retrieval + generation flows, return cached retrieval-only result and queue full gen asynchronously.
[03:20] Anika Rao: curious about backpressure — do you push back to clients or do you buffer at edge? we can't break our upstreams.
[03:26] Luis Ortega: best practice is to combine: push explicit 429 with Retry-After for user-facing APIs and also maintain a small edge buffer (seconds-scale) in the surge layer. that way orchestrated clients can retry, while UI clients get a graceful error.
[03:38] Tomás Alvarez: network considerations on our VPC: egress to hosted Redwood staging is restricted, plus HSM/KMS for key material. any blockers for KV cache synchronization in VPC?
[03:46] Rina Patel: for on-prem VPC, KV cache is local to each GPU pod; synchronization is not required. for shared warmup we can use a warmup orchestration that pushes prefix batches to each pod (via an internal S3 or NFS). KMS/HSM impacts key management for logs and model artifact signing only — shouldn't affect runtime caching.
[04:05] Maya Chen: one gotcha: prewarming all pods for every possible prefix is expensive. you want an adaptive approach: warm top heavy hitters continuously, and opportunistically warm others when you see them once (on first cold request we apply a faster warm path).
[04:20] Priya Kapoor: how quickly can that first-warm path complete? we worry p99 tail may be huge on first-touch.
[04:25] Luis Ortega: depends on sequence length; typical first-warm for a 4k prefix can add ~120-300ms extra startup; for 16k it's more. the surge-absorber helps by absorbing those initial spikes and protecting the reserved pool from the compounding cold-starts.
[04:40] Anika Rao: queueing numbers — can you share a reference table? like given arrival rate lambda and pool size c what p95 looks like?
[04:46] Rina Patel: yes — we'll share the sim sheet. short story: with admission policy tuned to keep utilization at 60-70% you'll hit the best latency/cost sweet spot; above 80% utilization the nonlinearity in queueing increases p95 very fast.
[05:00] Tomás Alvarez: do you support prioritized routing by endpoint? we need API A to always get priority over batch scoring.
[05:05] Luis Ortega: yes, multi-queue with weights is supported. priority queues plus weighted tickets allow per-endpoint SLOs.
[05:12] Maya Chen: we should also note impact of batching — larger batches increase throughput but increase tail for short requests. our runtime has dynamic batching that respects max latency budgets; we can set strict per-route max queue delay to avoid large batches for low-latency endpoints.
[05:27] Priya Kapoor: ok and for metrics/observability during a storm, what do you instrument?
[05:32] Rina Patel: token-level latency, queue depth per pool, KV hit ratio, prewarm fail rates, admission decisions and reasons, and ticket-pool utilization. we'll provide dashboards and tracing hooks.
[05:44] Anika Rao: security checklist — SOC2 and KMS integration, SSO, and audit logs — are these covered in Private deployment?
[05:50] Maya Chen: yes, Private deployments support SOC2 controls, SAML SSO via OIDC, and KMS/HSM integrations; we'll send the security pack.
[05:58] Tomás Alvarez: one more thing — benchmarking: we want a 24h replay of a recent burst window against your staging. is that feasible?
[06:03] Luis Ortega: absolutely, we can schedule. we'll need anonymized traces and an agreed replay window. we'll run with your quantization configs and two pool topologies (with and without surge-absorber) and report p50/p95/p99 and cost delta.
[06:18] Maya Chen: ok, wraps — quick recap and owners?
[06:22] Anika Rao: thanks everyone.
[06:24] (call ends)
